opening: I’m skipping placements to build my startup full time. I’ll regret it forever if I don’t try.

questions.q: What would you lose if it fails in 12 months?

choices.reply: A real cost, but a recoverable one. Seneca’s advice: rehearse the worst case, and it loses its grip on you.
choices.open: What’s your plan for month 13 if it fails?

choices.reply: Then it isn’t only your risk. Aristotle’s practical wisdom means weighing everyone your choice touches.
choices.open: Have you asked your family how much they’re willing to lose?

choices.reply: Being young lowers the cost; it doesn’t make it zero. A year is a year, and placements don’t come round twice.
choices.open: What would a year out cost you when you look for a job?

questions.q: Does anyone depend on your income?

choices.reply: That’s freedom, and it’s rarer than it looks. It makes this bet more yours to take.
choices.open: What’s the least you can live on for a year?

choices.reply: Then there’s a floor you can’t go below. Work out that number before you jump.
choices.open: What do your parents need from you each month?

choices.reply: Then you have a window. Windows are worth using, and worth knowing when they close.
choices.open: When does your window close?

questions.q: Has anyone paid for the product yet?

choices.reply: That’s evidence, not just hope. It makes the case for you stronger.
choices.open: Would they pay again, and tell a friend?

choices.reply: Then you’re betting on belief, not evidence. That’s allowed, but it’s worth knowing which one you’re using.
choices.open: What would it take to get one paying customer this month?

choices.reply: Then skipping placements buys you time to build, not proof. Could you build something first?
choices.open: Could you build a first version before placements end?

realQuestion: Is a secure path worth giving up for a chance you’d regret not taking?

caseFor.text: Courage is a virtue: acting well in spite of fear.
No rulebook chooses for you. You become who you are by choosing.

otherSide.point: Practical wisdom means weighing your circumstances, not just your desire.
Live the worst case for a few days first, so it can’t ambush you.
You’ll regret something either way, so regret alone can’t decide it.

pushbacks.say: But I’ll regret it forever if I don’t try.
pushbacks.reply: Kierkegaard would say you’ll regret something either way. Could you keep one offer open while you test for 8 weeks? Regret has a cheaper version.
pushbacks.test: Keep one offer open while you test for 8 weeks.

pushbacks.say: Everyone successful took a big risk.
pushbacks.reply: That’s survivorship: we hear from the risk-takers who made it, not the ones who didn’t. And Sartre would remind you that you’re choosing your life, not borrowing theirs.
pushbacks.test: Talk to two founders who tried and stopped. Ask what they’d do differently.

pushbacks.say: A job would kill my motivation.
pushbacks.reply: Maybe. But for Aristotle, courage is the brave thing done wisely, not just the brave thing. A deadline can protect motivation too.
pushbacks.test: Set a date and a number: if the startup hasn’t hit it by then, you take a job.

card.position: Skip placements to build my startup full time.
card.strong: Courage, and a story that’s yours to write.

opening: I got a job offer in another city. My parents want me to stay. I think I should go.

questions.q: What does staying give you that the job can’t?

choices.reply: That’s a real good, and a hard one to get back later. Worth weighing honestly.
choices.open: How much time with them would you actually lose?

choices.reply: A practical reason. But costs can be planned for; an offer like this might not come twice.
choices.open: Does the new salary cover the new city?

choices.reply: Then the question isn’t whether to leave. It’s how to leave well.
choices.open: What would leaving well look like?

questions.q: Do your parents need you there, or want you there?

choices.reply: Want matters, but it isn’t need. Mill would say their preferences can’t write your plan of life for you.
choices.open: How can you honour what they want without living by it?

choices.reply: That changes the weight of it. Aristotle says what we owe our parents can never be fully repaid, so it can’t be ignored.
choices.open: Who else could help with their care if you go?

choices.reply: Then that’s the first thing to find out. It’s hard to decide well without knowing which one it is.
choices.open: Is it want, or need?

questions.q: Could you come back if it doesn’t work out?

choices.reply: Then this is more reversible than it feels. Reversible choices deserve less agonising.
choices.open: What would make you come back?

choices.reply: A year is a real trial. Set it up as one, with a check-in point.
choices.open: What would you check at the one-year mark?

choices.reply: Then it’s a one-way door, and it deserves more care. Not a reason to stay; a reason to prepare.
choices.open: What would make a one-way move feel safe enough?

realQuestion: Whose life is this plan for: yours, theirs, or both?

caseFor.text: A plan of life chosen for you by others is barely yours.
You can’t hand this choice to a rule. It’s yours to make.

otherSide.point: While your parents are alive, don’t go far; if you must go, make sure they know where to find you.
What we owe our parents can never be fully repaid, so it can’t be ignored either.

pushbacks.say: But I can’t stay forever just because they want me to.
pushbacks.reply: Fair. Even Confucius left room: if you go, let them know where to find you. Could you agree on visits before you leave, instead of after the guilt?
pushbacks.test: Ask your parents what exactly they’re afraid of, before you decide.

pushbacks.reply: Maybe. Confucius asks for something smaller: that they know where to find you. Getting used to it goes faster with a plan than with silence.
pushbacks.test: Agree on a call schedule and the date of the first visit before you accept.

pushbacks.reply: Mill would agree it’s yours to live. Aristotle would add that a good life includes the people in it. Both can be true.
pushbacks.test: Ask your parents what exactly they’re afraid of, and answer each fear before you go.

card.position: Take the job in another city, against my parents’ wishes.
card.strong: A life you choose is more yours than one chosen for you.

opening: Honestly, money matters more than meaning. Meaning is what people talk about once rent is paid.

questions.q: What would more money get you?

choices.reply: That’s security, and it’s a real good. It’s also a specific amount, not an endless one.
choices.open: How much would end the rent stress?

choices.say: Out of a job I hate
choices.reply: So money is the exit, not the goal. That’s meaning, wearing a salary.
choices.open: What would you do the day you left?

choices.reply: Seneca would say that’s the one kind of wanting that never gets full.
choices.open: What would “more” be for?

choices.say: I’ll know when I see it
choices.reply: Most people don’t. The target tends to move as soon as they get close.
choices.open: What number is enough, and why that one?

choices.reply: Good. A number is a finish line, and finish lines can be crossed.
choices.open: Have you written the number down?

choices.reply: Epicurus would call that vanity talking: what we need is limited, what we want isn’t.
choices.open: Is there a number that would stop the worry?

questions.q: When did something last feel worth it, money aside?

choices.reply: Then meaning isn’t missing from your life. It’s just not the thing you’re counting.
choices.open: What was it, and how do you get more of it?

choices.reply: That’s worth sitting with. It might be the real problem under the money one.
choices.open: What used to feel worth it?

choices.reply: So you know what it feels like. What was different then: the work, or the people?
choices.open: What from college could you bring back?

realQuestion: Do you want money, or what you think it buys: freedom, safety, respect?

caseFor.text: A good life needs some means. Poverty makes it harder to live well.
You’re right that meaning is easier to discuss once rent is paid.

otherSide.point: Money is only ever useful for something else, so it can’t be the point.
What nature needs is limited and easy to get; what vanity wants never ends.
Poor isn’t having too little. It’s always wanting more.

pushbacks.say: But getting out of a job I hate is meaning, for me.
pushbacks.reply: Then you’ve found the real goal, and it has a number. Epicurus would say: work out what enough is, before the target moves.
pushbacks.test: Write down what enough is, in numbers, and what you’d do the day you hit it.

pushbacks.reply: True, and Aristotle agrees you need the means. He’d just say money is for something. Name the something, and you’ll know when to stop.
pushbacks.test: Write down what the money is for, and how much of it that takes.

pushbacks.reply: Some do. Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, and he still wrote that always wanting more is the real poverty.
pushbacks.test: For one month, note each purchase that still made you happier a week later.

card.strong: Security is a real good, and it comes before a lot of other goods.

opening: I’m building food delivery for college hostels. The big apps made it, so will I.

questions.q: Who pays: the students, or their parents?

choices.reply: Then every order competes with the canteen and a packet of instant noodles. Small baskets, thin margins.
choices.open: Can a small order cover the cost of delivering it?

choices.reply: Interesting. Parents pay for peace of mind, not speed. That’s a meal subscription, not a delivery app.
choices.open: Would parents prepay a month before seeing it work?

choices.reply: Normal at this stage, and the most important thing to find out. Who pays decides what you build.
choices.open: Who actually pays, and how much?

questions.q: What happens to orders during vacations?

choices.reply: Hostels sit empty for about three months a year. That’s a quarter of the year with costs and no customers.
choices.open: Can the business cover three empty months?

choices.reply: Then you’re up against the big apps on their home turf, where they’re strongest.
choices.open: Why would anyone pick you over the big apps at home?

choices.reply: Most people don’t. It’s also the usual way campus businesses quietly shut down.
choices.open: What happens to your riders when campus is empty?

questions.q: Why won’t students just call the local dhaba?

choices.reply: Faster matters at 11 p.m., when the dhaba’s shut. At lunch it’s a two-minute walk away.
choices.open: Is late night your whole market?

choices.reply: Cheaper than a place with no app, no riders and no commission? That’s hard to keep up.
choices.open: How are you cheaper once you pay the riders?

choices.reply: Choice helps, but students mostly reorder the same three things.
choices.open: Do students want choice, or the usual, fast?

realQuestion: Does demand survive three months of holidays a year?
bias: Survivorship. You’re looking at the big apps, not the graveyard.

caseFor.text: A captive audience, all in one place.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

caseFor.text: Dense routes: one building, hundreds of customers.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Couldn’t cover delivery costs on small orders.

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Lost to the hostel’s own mess contract.

pushbacks.say: But we’ll be faster than the dhaba.
pushbacks.reply: Then prove it where speed wins: late nights, one hostel, two weeks. If people order again, you’ve got something.
pushbacks.test: Run late-night delivery in one hostel for two weeks. Count the repeat orders.

pushbacks.say: The big apps did fine, so the demand is there.
pushbacks.reply: The demand is there, and so are the big apps. The startups on the other side had demand too. What they lacked was a reason to be picked over the default.
pushbacks.test: Ask 30 students which app they ordered from last week, and what would make them switch.

pushbacks.say: Vacations won’t matter if we grow fast.
pushbacks.reply: Growth doesn’t fill an empty campus. It just makes the empty months more expensive. Plan the quiet months first.
pushbacks.test: Price out three vacation months: riders, rent, and zero orders. See if you’re still standing.

card.strong: A dense, captive audience that’s cheap to reach.

opening: An app that splits rent and bills between flatmates. Everyone fights about money, so everyone needs it.

questions.q: How do flatmates split bills today?

choices.say: A group chat and a spreadsheet
choices.reply: So it’s already solved, for free, with tools everyone has. Your app has to beat “good enough”.
choices.open: What does the spreadsheet get wrong often enough to pay to fix?

choices.reply: That person is your customer. Everyone else in the flat is just along for the ride.
choices.open: Would the one who chases pay, even if the rest won’t?

choices.reply: Fights are loud, but they’re not a budget. People rarely pay to end an argument they can just keep having.
choices.open: Is the fight about the maths, or about who didn’t pay?

choices.reply: A monthly fee to split a monthly bill. Every flatmate has to agree it’s worth it.
choices.open: Will a whole flat agree to pay, or only one person?

choices.reply: Landlords already get paid. What problem of theirs would you solve?
choices.open: What does a landlord lose when flatmates fight?

choices.reply: Ads need lots of people opening the app lots of times. Bills come once a month.
choices.open: How many flats would ads need to cover your costs?

questions.q: How often does a flat need it?

choices.reply: Good, that’s a habit. Now it has to be less effort than the group chat it replaces, every month.
choices.open: Is it less effort than the group chat, every single month?

choices.reply: Then it’s used a few times a year. Hard to charge monthly for that.
choices.open: Could it be a one-time tool for moving in and out?

choices.reply: Then you’re selling to people at their angriest, once. Tough market.
choices.open: After a fight, do people look for tools, or just avoid each other?

realQuestion: Is the pain big enough to pay for, or just big enough to complain about?
bias: Availability. The fights are memorable, so they feel more common than they are.

caseFor.text: Money fights are real, and they come back every month.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

caseFor.text: A clear moment of need: rent day.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

caseFor.text: It spreads itself: one flatmate invites the rest.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Used for a month, then everyone went back to the group chat.

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Needed every flatmate to sign up. Most flats had one holdout.

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Charging for what a spreadsheet does free didn’t stick.

pushbacks.say: But ours will be much simpler.
pushbacks.reply: Simpler than a group chat is a high bar. Would a flat pay to stop using theirs? Ask ten flats before you build.
pushbacks.test: Track bills by hand for ten flats for a month. See how many would pay to keep it.

pushbacks.say: Everyone I know complains about this.
pushbacks.reply: Complaining is free. That’s the availability bias again: the fights stick in memory, the calm months don’t. Find out who’d pay.
pushbacks.test: Ask 20 flats to prepay one month. Count how many actually do.

pushbacks.say: We’ll make it fun, with reminders and badges.
pushbacks.reply: Fun helps people come back, but nobody wants a game about owing rent. Fix the chasing first; the badges can wait.
pushbacks.test: Send the reminders by hand for five flats for a month. See if the chasing stops.

card.strong: A real, monthly pain with a built-in way to spread.

opening: I’m proposing we build our own customer database instead of paying for one. We’d save the subscription.

questions.q: How many people would use it?

choices.reply: Eight people: small enough that a paid tool is cheap, big enough that a day of downtime really hurts.
choices.open: What does a day of downtime cost eight salespeople?

choices.reply: Then it’s not a side project anymore. Everyone’s work would run through code a few people maintain.
choices.open: Who fixes it when the whole company is stuck?

choices.reply: Then the subscription is probably tiny, and a spreadsheet might do. Why build at all?
choices.open: Would a spreadsheet do the job for now?

questions.q: Who keeps it running after launch?

choices.reply: So two developers who aren’t working on your actual product. That’s the real price tag.
choices.open: What would those developers build instead?

choices.reply: Then you’re paying a subscription again, just to a different company, and with less control.
choices.open: Is an agency retainer cheaper than the tool?

choices.reply: Every internal tool says that at launch. Security updates, new fields, broken imports: it adds up.
choices.open: Who owns it when the person who built it leaves?

questions.q: What does the current tool cost a year?

choices.reply: Then the build only pays off if it takes under a month, and never needs fixing. It won’t.
choices.open: How many months would the build really take?

choices.reply: Now it’s a fair comparison. But the build costs a salary too, plus the upkeep after.
choices.open: Is there a cheaper plan of the tool you have?

choices.reply: Worth finding out before the pitch. It’s the first thing your boss will ask.
choices.open: What does the current tool actually cost?

realQuestion: Is the subscription the real cost, or the developer time it takes to keep a new one alive?
bias: Planning fallacy. First versions always look cheaper than they turn out.

caseFor.text: You’d own your data and your workflow.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

caseFor.text: No per-seat fees as the team grows.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

caseFor.text: It could fit your sales process exactly.
caseFor.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: The one developer who understood it left.

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Upkeep cost more hours than the subscription did.

otherSide.source: Illustrative business assumption — not a verified company history
otherSide.point: Went back to a paid tool after missing a quarter’s reports.

pushbacks.say: But our needs are really specific.
pushbacks.reply: Then list the three things the current tool can’t do. If a setting or add-on covers them, the build solves a problem you don’t have.
pushbacks.test: List the three things the current tool can’t do, and check whether a setting or add-on does them.

pushbacks.reply: A good reason. Most paid tools let you export everything, though. If yours does, you own your data already.
pushbacks.test: Export everything from the current tool this week. See what, if anything, you can’t take with you.

pushbacks.reply: That’s a real cost. Compare it with developer time, not with zero. Then ask the vendor for a better plan.
pushbacks.test: Get a quote for a smaller plan, and price the build as developer hours plus a year of upkeep.

card.position: Build our own customer database instead of paying for one.
card.strong: Ownership, no per-seat fees, and a perfect fit.
